newsitem.title: JAPAN: FUND VIEW -- Japan foresees business as usual in HK.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW -- Japan foresees business as usual in HK.

text.p: The July 1 return of Hong Kong to China may be the end of an era for some, but for Japanese investors, who have spent heavily in the colony, it will be business as usual, fund managers say.
They say there will be no change in their Hong Kong investment strategies in the short term, and even in the long term they see prospects as bright, although they confess to some uncertainty.

"Even if there is some friction, we don't think there will be much change... If they really changed Hong Kong, the handover would become meaningless," said Joji Maki, general manager at Nikko Securities Investment Trust & Management.
For Japan's investment trust management funds, the question of Hong Kong's future is a significant one.

Their stock holdings in the territory, which make up virtually their entire investment there, stood at around 204 billion yen at the end of February 1997 out of their roughly 816 billion yen in foreign stock holdings. The figure is second only to their holdings in the United States.

A year earlier, their Hong Kong stock holdings were nearly 305 billion yen out of their 884 billion yen in foreign stocks, but fund managers said the reduction was due to Asian market factors and not to nerves about the territory's return to China. Their stock holdings in Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia also decreased.

Fund managers said they saw the handover ultimately as a plus in many ways, citing expectations of capital inflows from China to bolster the real estate and stock markets, as well as general economic stimulus from closer ties and greater access to the huge Chinese market.

But they said they were looking most eagerly at wider opportunities for investment, not only in traditional Hong Kong economic pillars such as finance and real estate, but also in "red chip", or China-linked, stocks.

"Everyone is looking at the red chips right now, as it's almost a matter of course for some of these to have growth as high as 30 to 40 percent," said Masamitsu Sato, a fund manager at Yamaichi Investment Trust Management.
He added that interest was strong irrespective of sector and that investment was focused on companies with backing from a strong parent company that had plenty of capital.

Sato said, and others agreed, that while there had been some capital flow out of Hong Kong since the beginning of this year, this was due more to overall market conditions in both Hong Kong and Asia in general than concern about the handover.
"The overall weighting of Asian holdings was high last year, with good performances, but in the last few months all the Asian markets have been doing rather poorly," he added.

A chilling concern for Hong Kong, whose currency is pegged to the dollar, was the impact of last month's U.S. interest rate rise, which sent stocks tumbling. The prospect of further rises remains an inhibiting factor.

"There has been some capital flowing out of Hong Kong to other ASEAN countries since the start of the year, especially after the U.S. interest rate rise, and further changes in interest rates could have quite an impact over the short term," said Osamu Yamashita, a fund manager at Daiwa Asset Management.

He said countries such as Singapore and the Philippines could be temporary beneficiaries of this movement in capital, although Daiwa had no plans to change its investments in Hong Kong substantially over the next six months to one year.
ASEAN, the Association of South East Asian Nations, comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

Although concern has arisen recently about the political situation in post-handover Hong Kong, particularly over restrictions to civil liberties, none of the fund managers felt this was likely to affect their investments significantly.
Several said one major concern was whether China would continue to allow free-market competition rather than the managed-market systems more typical of Communist countries.

Others said they would closely watch the Chinese Communist Party Congress later this year. "We need to see clues as to who may succeed (President) Jiang Zemin. And if it doesn't go too well in those terms, there may be a bit of a shock to investment," said Nikko Securities' Maki.
But he added: "We're much more concerned with the economy than with politics, and as long as nothing drastic happens in terms of human rights it's unlikely to be a problem."
